research.approach: Salon practitioners combine four levers in a set order: measure the no-shows and who they come from, set a clear and fair cancellation policy, remind clients more than once in a way that lets them cancel easily, and put a financial commitment (card capture or deposit) on the riskiest bookings first, such as new clients, past no-shows, long services and peak slots, rather than on everyone. Regular clients are protected by telling them personally first, using gentler fee rules for them, and waiving fees for real emergencies. In the UK the terms must be fair and clear before the client commits: fees should reflect the salon's real loss and rise on a sliding scale, and a deposit should be small, not a penalty. The effect is read over weeks, not days, with the regulars' rebooking watched as the guardrail.

sources.title: Fresha Help Centre: Set up payment policies
sources.note: Page is undated; date is when it was read (2026-11-02). Deposits or card capture, free-cancellation window, late and no-show fee percentages, apply to client groups such as new clients or past no-shows, per service, minimum value.

sources.title: How to protect your business against no-shows and late cancellations (Fresha)
sources.note: Vendor blog, published 2022-03 and shown as last updated 2026-11-02. Up to two reminders at 3, 24, 48 or 72 hours; show the policy at booking; blocking online booking is a last resort. Its percentage claims are vendor claims.

sources.title: Deposits vs cancellation fees: which reduces no-shows faster? (Goldie)
sources.note: Vendor blog. Deposits act faster, especially for new clients and long services; fees are gentler for loyal clients; publish the policy and repeat it in confirmations; waive for genuine emergencies. No data on how much no-shows fall.

sources.title: Refund and cancellation terms for UK hair salons (Sprintlaw)
sources.note: Law firm article, not legal advice. Terms should be fair, transparent and shown before the client is bound; charges proportionate to real loss; say what happens if the salon cancels; keep records.

sources.title: CMA: Wedding venues advised to play fair
sources.note: Official advice for another sector, used by analogy: a deposit should only reserve the booking and be a small share of the price, and cancellation charges should follow a sliding scale that reflects likely loss.

steps.name: Measure the no-shows and who they come from
steps.why: An 18% average hides who is missing: new clients, a few repeat no-showers, long services or certain days. Splitting no-shows from late cancellations and counting by client type, day, time, service and lead time shows where a rule will help and where it would hit regulars.

steps.name: Set a clear, fair cancellation policy before any fee
steps.why: Clients must see the free-cancellation window and the fees before they commit. Fees follow a sliding scale tied to the salon's real loss, a deposit stays small, and the policy says what happens if the salon cancels. Fresha generates the cancellation terms from the policy settings.

steps.name: Send reminders earlier and more than once, with an easy way to cancel
steps.why: One reminder at 24 hours leaves little time to refill a slot. Practitioners send a second reminder, such as at 48 hours as well as 24, repeat the policy in confirmations and make cancelling easy.

steps.name: Put a card or deposit on the riskiest bookings first
steps.why: Card capture or a small deposit works best on new clients, clients with past no-shows, long services and peak slots, and can be limited to those client groups so regulars are not hit.

steps.name: Tell regular clients personally first and allow for emergencies
steps.why: Loyal clients take rules better when they hear them directly, see them in every confirmation and know genuine emergencies are waived. Blocking online booking is the last step, after other efforts.

steps.name: Switch changes on in stages and read the effect weekly
steps.why: Changes are introduced one at a time, each recorded with its date, so the effect on no-shows and on regulars can be told apart. Results are read over weeks.

pitfalls.text: Charging a large non-refundable deposit or a flat full-price penalty, which can be unfair under consumer law.
Writing strict rules for clients but nothing about what happens when the salon cancels or moves an appointment.
Applying a deposit or card rule to everyone, including long-standing regulars, instead of the riskiest groups.
Bookings made by staff default to no policy in Fresha, so the rules do not apply unless the setting is checked.
Treating vendor percentages as promises, and judging after a week or two.

hypotheses.statement: Most no-shows come from new clients and a small group of repeat no-showers.
hypotheses.test: No-show rate and share of all no-shows by new clients, returning clients and clients with two or more earlier no-shows.
hypotheses.confirm_if: These groups make up a large share of no-shows while being a small share of appointments.
hypotheses.refute_if: No-shows are spread evenly across client types.

hypotheses.statement: Regular clients also no-show enough that rules aimed at new clients will not reach the target.
hypotheses.test: Regular clients' no-show and late-cancellation rate and their share of all no-shows, under the fixed regular definition.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Regular clients account for a large share of no-shows.

hypotheses.statement: A single reminder 24 hours before is too late or too hard to act on.
hypotheses.test: No-show and late-cancellation rate by reminder status and by how long before the appointment the client last changed the booking.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Many no-shows had no earlier chance to be refilled, or clients without a reminder no-show more.
hypotheses.refute_if: Reminded and unreminded clients no-show at similar rates.

hypotheses.statement: Appointments booked far ahead are missed more often.
hypotheses.test: No-show rate by days between booking and appointment.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The rate rises clearly with lead time.
hypotheses.refute_if: The rate is flat across lead times.

hypotheses.statement: Certain services, stylists, days or times carry most of the lost value.
hypotheses.test: No-show rate and lost price by service, stylist, weekday and time slot, with volume noted.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A few services or slots with enough volume account for a large share of the lost value.
hypotheses.refute_if: Rates and lost value are even.

hypotheses.statement: With no card or deposit, clients face no cost for missing an appointment.
hypotheses.test: Compare no-show rates for clients who booked through staff, who have no policy by default, and online; look for any history of cancellation fees.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Groups with no commitment no-show far more than groups with any commitment.
hypotheses.refute_if: Rates are similar with or without any commitment.

hypotheses.statement: The 18% is overstated because late cancellations or unmarked appointments are counted as no-shows.
hypotheses.test: Re-count the 18% under the written definition and check how staff mark missed appointments.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The re-count under the written definition is clearly lower than 18%.

measurement.window: Weekly over the two months, read as four-week rates; judge each change only after enough weeks following its date.
measurement.min_volume: Judge group rates only with the number of appointments agreed with the owner before the first read; smaller groups are INCONCLUSIVE.
measurement.stop_rule: Pause the newest rule if regular clients' rebooking falls or clients complain it is unfair; otherwise keep each rule for its full window.
